## Overview

c-ward could be extended to be ABI-compatible with different platforms, however currently it is only known to be ABI-compatible with `*-unknown-linux-gnu*` platforms.(no content)The primary way this is used is through Mustang and Eyra, as their libc implementations. It can also be used as a regular library in "coexist-with-libc" mode.

## How It Works

The project uses a modular architecture with **c-gull** as a key component:

The goal is to have very little code in c-gull itself, by factoring out all of the significant functionality into independent crates with more Rust-idiomatic APIs, with c-gull just wrapping those APIs to implement the C ABIs.

### Two Operating Modes

c-gull has two main cargo features: "take-charge" and "coexist-with-libc". One of these must be enabled. In "take-charge" mode, c-gull takes charge of the process, handling program startup (via Origin) providing malloc (via c-scape), and other things. This requires some additional setup.(no content)In "coexist-with-libc" mode, c-gull can be used as a drop-in (partial) libc replacement. To use it, just change your typical libc dependency in Cargo.toml and c-gull will replace as many of the system libc implementation with its own implementations as it can. In particular, it can't replace malloc or any of the pthread functions in this configuration, but it can replace many other things.

## Key Technical Details

By being implemented entirely in Rust, avoiding libc, errno, and pthread cancellation, and employing some specialized optimizations, most functions compile down to very efficient code, which can often be fully inlined into user code. Most functions in linux_raw preserve memory, I/O safety, and pointer provenance all the way down to the syscalls.(no content)Rustix uses libc, via the libc crate, except on Linux, where it uses raw system calls.

### Compiler Considerations

Normally, a libc implementation would use `#[no_builtins]` to prevent compilers from noticing the bodies of libc functions implement the semantics of libc functions and replacing them with calls, which effectively makes them uselessly recursive calls to themselves.

## Current Status

This is currently highly experimental, incomplete, and some things aren't optimized.(no content)And it depends on Nightly Rust.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about using Eyra (by sunfishcode) without a custom target:

## Eyra Overview

Eyra is similar to Mustang and uses the same underlying code, but instead of using a custom target and -Z build-std, Eyra just needs users to add -nostartfiles to their link line, such as via build.rs in the example.

## How to Set Up a Project

You need two key files:

### 1. build.rs
A build.rs file to add -nostartfiles to the link flags to disable the host startup code, so that Eyra can provide its own:

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-nostartfiles");
}
```

With that, cargo build, cargo run, cargo test (with Nightly) and so on will work normally with any *-unknown-linux-gnu* target.

### 2. main.rs
You need to add a dependency on `eyra` in your Cargo.toml and reference it in main.rs.

Under the covers, it's using Origin to start and stop the program, c-ward to handle libc calls from std, and rustix to do the printing, so it's completely implemented in Rust.(no content)For an example of the above steps, check out this hello world example.

## Comparison to Mustang

Eyra uses the same underlying libraries as Mustang, but doesn't use a custom target, and doesn't need -Z build-std.

## Platform Support

Eyra currently runs on Nightly Rust on Linux on x86-64, x86, aarch64, and riscv64. It aims to support all Linux versions supported by Rust, though at this time it's only tested on relatively recent versions.

## Static Linking Options

Eyra executables don't depend on any dynamic libraries, however by default they do still depend on a dynamic linker (eg. "/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"). For fully static linking, build with `RUSTFLAGS=-C target-feature=+crt-static -C relocation-model=static`. This disables Position-Independent Executable (PIE) mode, which is straightforward, however it loses the security benefits of Address-Space Layout Randomization (ASLR).

You can find the official hello world example at: https://github.com/sunfishcode/eyra

# Eyra main.rs Example

Based on the documentation, a minimal `main.rs` with Eyra requires **no special attributes or macros** for the basic case:

```rust
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```

This is standard Rust code. The magic happens in two other places:

## Required Setup

1. **Cargo.toml dependency:**
   ```toml
   cargo add eyra --rename=std
   ```

2. **build.rs file:**
   ```rust
   fn main() {
       println!("cargo:rustc-link-arg=-nostartfiles");
   }
   ```

The `-nostartfiles` flag disables the host's startup code, allowing Eyra to provide its own program initialization instead.

## Alternative (with `-Zbuild-std`)

If using the unstable `-Zbuild-std` feature, you would add a different dependency and include this in `main.rs`:

```rust
extern crate eyra;
```

This ensures Eyra's libraries are linked in when using `-Zbuild-std`.

**Bottom line:** Your application code stays normal Rust—Eyra's integration happens through build configuration, not code annotations.
